title: Classification Algorithms
summary: Classification predicts categories - spam or not, disease or healthy, which digit. Different algorithms make different assumptions: logistic regression draws linear boundaries, decision trees split on features, KNN uses proximity, and SVMs find optim
content:
# Classification Algorithms ##### The cancer screening model that detected nothing A team built a model to flag mammograms for radiologist review. In their dataset, 0.8% of scans showed cancer. The model achieved **99.2% accuracy**, and the team celebrated. Then someone examined the predictions. The model had learned to output "no cancer" for every single scan. On a dataset that is 99.2% negative, always predicting negative gives 99.2% accuracy — and detects zero cancers. Accuracy is the default metric, the one everyone reaches for first, and on imbalanced problems it is actively misleading. The failure here was not the algorithm; it was the evaluation. Classification is the most common task in applied ML, and **choosing the right metric matters more than choosing the right algorithm.** ##### Logistic regression Despite the name, logistic regression is a classifier. It fits a linear combination of features, then squashes the result into a probability between 0 and 1 using the **sigmoid** function: ```text z = w₁x₁ + w₂x₂ + ... + b P(y=1) = 1 / (1 + e^(−z)) ``` ```python import numpy as np from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler from sklearn.pipeline import make_pipeline from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split from sklearn.datasets import make_classification X, y = make_classification(n_samples=2000, n_features=10, n_informative=6, weights=[0.85, 0.15], random_state=42) X_tr, X_te, y_tr, y_te = train_test_split(X, y, test_size=0.25, random_state=42, stratify=y) clf = make_pipeline(StandardScaler(), LogisticRegression(max_iter=1000)).fit(X_tr, y_tr) probabilities = clf.predict_proba(X_te)[:, 1] # probability of class 1 predictions = clf.predict(X_te) # applies a 0.5 threshold ``` Two properties make logistic regression the right first model for almost any classification problem. It outputs **calibrated probabilities**, not just labels — which lets you set your own decision threshold rather than accepting 0.5. And its **coefficients are interpretable**: exponentiating one gives an odds ratio, so a coefficient of 0.7 means that feature multiplies the odds by `e^0.7 ≈ 2.0`. It draws a **linear decision boundary**, which is its main limitation. If the classes are separated by a curve, logistic regression will underfit. ##### Decision trees A decision tree asks a sequence of yes/no questions, splitting the data at each step: ```python from sklearn.tree import DecisionTreeClassifier, export_text tree = DecisionTreeClassifier(max_depth=4, min_samples_leaf=20, random_state=42) tree.fit(X_tr, y_tr) print(export_text(tree, max_depth=2)) print(f"train {tree.score(X_tr, y_tr):.3f} test {tree.score(X_te, y_te):.3f}") ``` The tree chooses each split to maximize purity, measured by **Gini impurity** or **entropy**. Both quantify how mixed the classes are in a node; the split that separates them best wins. Strengths: no scaling needed, handles nonlinear boundaries and feature interactions naturally, mixes numeric and categorical data, and is genuinely explainable — you can print the rules. The critical weakness: **an unconstrained tree memorizes the training data.** Left to grow, it creates a leaf for every sample and achieves 100% training accuracy with poor generalization. The constraints that prevent this — `max_depth`, `min_samples_leaf`, `min_samples_split` — are not optional. This weakness is why **Random Forests** exist: train many trees on random subsets of data and features, then average their votes. Individual trees overfit in different directions and the errors cancel. A Random Forest is usually a strong baseline with almost no tuning. ##### K-Nearest Neighbors KNN makes no model at all. To classify a point, it finds the `k` closest training examples and takes a majority vote: ```python from sklearn.neighbors import KNeighborsClassifier knn = make_pipeline(StandardScaler(), KNeighborsClassifier(n_neighbors=15)).fit(X_tr, y_tr) ``` **Scaling is mandatory** — KNN computes distances, so a feature ranging 0–100,000 will dominate one ranging 0–1 entirely. The `k` value controls the bias-variance balance directly: `k=1` fits every training point exactly (high variance), while large `k` smooths toward predicting the majority class (high bias). Odd values avoid ties in binary problems. KNN is intuitive and needs no training, but prediction is slow — every query compares against the whole training set — and it degrades badly in high dimensions, where distances between points become nearly uniform. Useful for small datasets and as a conceptual reference point; rarely the production choice. ##### Support Vector Machines An SVM finds the decision boundary with the **widest margin** between classes — the boundary as far as possible from the nearest points of each class (Cortes & Vapnik, 1995). Those nearest points are the **support vectors**, and they alone determine the boundary. ```python from sklearn.svm import SVC svm_linear = make_pipeline(StandardScaler(), SVC(kernel="linear", C=1.0)).fit(X_tr, y_tr) svm_rbf = make_pipeline(StandardScaler(), SVC(kernel="rbf", C=1.0, gamma="scale", probability=True)).fit(X_tr, y_tr) ``` The **kernel trick** is what makes SVMs powerful: an RBF kernel implicitly maps data into a much higher-dimensional space where a linear boundary exists, without ever computing those coordinates. The result is a flexible curved boundary in the original space. Two hyperparameters matter. **`C`** controls the tradeoff between a wide margin and misclassifying training points — low `C` means a smoother, more regularized boundary. **`gamma`** controls how far each point's influence reaches; high gamma produces tight, wiggly boundaries that overfit. SVMs work well on small-to-medium datasets with clear margins, but training scales poorly beyond roughly 100,000 samples, and `probability=True` is slow because it requires internal cross-validation. ##### The confusion matrix Every classification metric derives from four counts: ```python from sklearn.metrics import confusion_matrix, classification_report tn, fp, fn, tp = confusion_matrix(y_te, predictions).ravel() print(f"TN {tn} FP {fp} FN {fn} TP {tp}") ``` ```text Predicted Negative Positive Actual Negative TN FP ← false alarm (Type I error) Actual Positive FN TP ← MISSED case (Type II error) ``` From these: ```text Accuracy = (TP + TN) / total — overall correctness Precision = TP / (TP + FP) — of those flagged, how many were right? Recall = TP / (TP + FN) — of the actual positives, how many did we catch? F1 = 2 · (P · R) / (P + R) — harmonic mean of precision and recall ``` In the mammogram story, the model had 99.2% accuracy and **0% recall** — it caught none of the actual cancers. Recall is the metric that would have exposed the failure immediately. **Precision versus recall is a genuine tradeoff**, and which matters depends entirely on the cost of each error type: | Scenario | Priority | Why | |---|---|---| | **Cancer screening** | **Recall** | A missed cancer is catastrophic; a false alarm costs one extra test | | **Spam filtering** | **Precision** | A legitimate email in the spam folder is worse than a spam email in the inbox | | **Fraud detection** | **Recall**, then precision | Missing fraud costs money; investigate the false positives | | **Recommendations** | **Precision** | Bad suggestions erode trust; missing one good item is invisible | Always print the full report rather than a single number: ```python print(classification_report(y_te, predictions, target_names=["negative", "positive"], digits=3)) ``` ##### The threshold, ROC and AUC `predict()` applies a 0.5 threshold, but that is a *choice*, not a law. Lowering it catches more positives at the cost of more false alarms: ```python for threshold in (0.2, 0.3, 0.5, 0.7): preds = (probabilities >= threshold).astype(int) tn, fp, fn, tp = confusion_matrix(y_te, preds).ravel() precision = tp / (tp + fp) if tp + fp else 0 recall = tp / (tp + fn) print(f"threshold {threshold}: precision {precision:.3f} recall {recall:.3f}") ``` The **ROC curve** plots true positive rate against false positive rate across every threshold, and **AUC** is the area beneath it: ```python from sklearn.metrics import roc_curve, roc_auc_score, average_precision_score import matplotlib.pyplot as plt fpr, tpr, _ = roc_curve(y_te, probabilities) auc = roc_auc_score(y_te, probabilities) fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6, 5)) ax.plot(fpr, tpr, linewidth=2, label=f"ROC (AUC = {auc:.3f})") ax.plot([0, 1], [0, 1], "k--", alpha=0.4, label="Random (AUC = 0.5)") ax.set_xlabel("False positive rate"); ax.set_ylabel("True positive rate") ax.legend(); ax.grid(alpha=0.3) ``` AUC has a clean interpretation: **the probability that a randomly chosen positive is ranked above a randomly chosen negative.** 0.5 is random guessing, 1.0 is perfect. Because it evaluates across all thresholds, it measures *ranking quality* independently of where you set the cut. One important caveat: **on heavily imbalanced data, prefer the precision–recall curve.** ROC-AUC can look reassuringly high when the negative class is enormous, because the false positive rate has a huge denominator. Average precision (the area under the PR curve) is the more honest number: ```python print(f"ROC-AUC {roc_auc_score(y_te, probabilities):.3f}") print(f"Avg precision {average_precision_score(y_te, probabilities):.3f}") ``` ##### Handling class imbalance Three approaches, and they combine: **Class weights** — tell the algorithm that errors on the minority class cost more. Simple, no data duplication, and supported by most scikit-learn classifiers: ```python clf = LogisticRegression(class_weight="balanced", max_iter=1000) ``` **Resampling** — oversample the minority class or undersample the majority. **SMOTE** (Chawla et al., 2002) generates synthetic minority examples by interpolating between neighbours rather than duplicating: ```python from imblearn.over_sampling import SMOTE from imblearn.pipeline import Pipeline as ImbPipeline pipeline = ImbPipeline([ ("scale", StandardScaler()), ("smote", SMOTE(random_state=42)), # applied to TRAINING folds only ("clf", LogisticRegression(max_iter=1000)), ]) ``` **Use `imblearn`'s Pipeline, not scikit-learn's.** This is a real trap: resampling must happen inside each cross-validation fold, on training data only. Applying SMOTE before splitting means synthetic points derived from test samples end up in training — leakage that inflates your scores substantially. **Threshold tuning** — often the simplest and most effective. Train normally, then choose the threshold that gives the recall your problem requires. ```mermaid flowchart TD A[Classification problem] --> B{Class balance?} B -->|balanced| C[Accuracy + F1 acceptable] B -->|imbalanced| D[Use precision, recall,
PR-AUC — never accuracy alone] C --> E[Baseline: logistic regression
scaled, interpretable] D --> E E --> F{Good enough?} F -->|underfit| G[Random Forest / SVM-RBF
nonlinear boundary] F -->|imbalanced recall too low| H[class_weight / SMOTE
/ lower threshold] G --> I[Compare on the SAME metric] H --> I I --> J[Confusion matrix + ROC/PR curve
choose operating threshold] ``` ##### Comparing the algorithms ```python from sklearn.ensemble import RandomForestClassifier from sklearn.model_selection import cross_val_score models = { "Logistic": make_pipeline(StandardScaler(), LogisticRegression(max_iter=1000)), "Decision Tree": DecisionTreeClassifier(max_depth=6, min_samples_leaf=20, random_state=42), "KNN": make_pipeline(StandardScaler(), KNeighborsClassifier(15)), "SVM (RBF)": make_pipeline(StandardScaler(), SVC(kernel="rbf")), "Random Forest": RandomForestClassifier(n_estimators=300, random_state=42), } for name, model in models.items(): scores = cross_val_score(model, X_tr, y_tr, cv=5, scoring="f1") print(f"{name:<15} F1 {scores.mean():.3f} ± {scores.std():.3f}") ``` | Algorithm | Boundary | Scaling | Interpretable | Best for | |---|---|---|---|---| | Logistic regression | Linear | Required | High | Baseline, probabilities, explanation | | Decision tree | Axis-aligned | No | High | Rules, mixed data types | | KNN | Local | Required | Low | Small data, conceptual reference | | SVM (RBF) | Flexible curve | Required | Low | Small/medium, clear margins | | Random Forest | Complex | No | Medium | Strong default on tabular data | Report a **mean and standard deviation** from cross-validation, not a single split's score. A model scoring 0.84 ± 0.02 is meaningfully more trustworthy than one scoring 0.85 ± 0.09. ##### Common mistakes - **Accuracy on imbalanced data** — the mammogram failure. - **Never inspecting the confusion matrix**, so you cannot see *which* errors occur. - **Accepting the 0.5 threshold** without asking what error costs. - **Forgetting to scale** for KNN, SVM and regularized logistic regression. - **Unconstrained decision trees**, which memorize training data. - **SMOTE applied before the train/test split**, leaking synthetic test information. - **ROC-AUC on severely imbalanced problems**, where PR-AUC is more informative. - **Comparing models on different metrics.** - **A single train/test split** rather than cross-validation with a reported spread. - **No baseline** — always check what a majority-class predictor achieves. ##### Your hands-on tie-in The practical task: train **logistic regression, a decision tree, KNN and SVM** on a classification dataset and compare **precision, recall and F1**. Use a deliberately imbalanced dataset and include accuracy in your table alongside the others — watching accuracy stay high while recall collapses is the most efficient way to internalize why the metric choice matters. The mini project is a **customer churn predictor** that **handles class imbalance** and produces a **confusion matrix and ROC curve** to justify the chosen model. The justification is the substance: state the business cost of a missed churner versus a wasted retention offer, then pick the operating threshold that reflects that ratio. A model chosen with an explicit cost argument is a far stronger portfolio piece than one chosen by highest F1. For the assignment, **explain precision versus recall and give a scenario where recall matters more**. Cancer screening is the canonical example, but make the reasoning explicit rather than asserting it: a false negative means an undetected tumour that grows for another year, while a false positive means an additional test that is unpleasant and expensive but not dangerous. When the costs of the two error types are that asymmetric, the metric — and the threshold — must reflect it. ##### Key takeaways - Accuracy is misleading on imbalanced data; always inspect the confusion matrix and report precision, recall and F1. - Logistic regression is the right first model — calibrated probabilities, interpretable coefficients, linear boundary — with Random Forest as the strong nonlinear default. - Scale features for KNN, SVM and regularized logistic regression; trees and forests do not need it. - The 0.5 threshold is a choice: tune it to the relative cost of false positives versus false negatives in your problem. - Handle imbalance with class weights, SMOTE inside an `imblearn` Pipeline, or threshold tuning — and use PR-AUC rather than ROC-AUC when positives are rare.
